extracted.intended_audience: feature writers, editors, journalism educators, and aspiring narrative journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for producing journalistic feature stories (narrative nonfiction, essays, first-person pieces) — what makes work eligible, memorable, and prize-worthy in feature journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature story definition (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Would you limit your definition to nonfiction narratives that maintain a measure of objectivity and rely on observation, scenes and dialogue? Or would you broaden it to include essays, columns, advocacy journalism and first-person pieces?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece recounts the debate among judges about what counts as a feature; since 2016 magazines became eligible across journalism categories, expanding the tent to include magazine-style and first-person work. Be open to a fluid definition — features can be traditional nonfiction narratives or broader forms that still produce meaningful, memorable work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on observation, scenes, and dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature storytelling that relies on observation, scenes and dialogue to show events and people rather than summarizing or telling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saslow emphasizes stories that unfold almost entirely in dialogue and scene to create a direct interaction between reader and subject. This technique helps readers 'see' the story and feel like they drew conclusions themselves. Anti-pattern: heavy exposition that tells rather than shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of writer presence / point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the writer's presence is felt (first-person, reflective) or minimized (objective, 'pane of glass' approach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saslow prefers minimal narrator presence so readers watch events through a clear pane of glass; others (recent winners) use first-person reflection and analysis effectively. Both approaches are acceptable — judges value work that uses the chosen stance well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making big issues feel personal
rubrics_metrics.description: Take big national or systemic issues (tension points, fissures) and make them feel personal and immediate through individual stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saslow looks for 'big tension points in the country' made personal in ways that illuminate them anew. Good features connect the macro and micro on a human level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition, meaningfulness, and memorability
rubrics_metrics.description: Work should be big, ambitious, meaningful and memorable — the kind of reporting writers aspire to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DeGregory and Saslow stress that features signal time investment and ambition. Judges look for stories that matter and that the reporter clearly invested significant time and craft into producing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid writing and narrative craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong, vivid prose and narrative craft that capture readers and render scenes and characters with clarity and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of winners emphasize 'vivid writing' and masterful braiding of elements. Narrative techniques (structure, pacing, scene-setting) should be deployed to maximum effect; poor craft (flat prose, weak scenes) undermines impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough reporting and sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting should be rigorous, thorough, and handled with sensitivity, especially on fraught subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Winners like Mitchell S. Jackson and Jennifer Senior combined thorough reporting with sensitive handling of subjects, including personal connection when relevant. Sensitive topics require careful sourcing and empathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personal experience when it adds value
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person or personal experience is appropriate when the reporter's perspective or role materially contributes to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several recent winners employed personal experience effectively (e.g., Jackson, Senior). DeGregory notes that when the reporter is a participant or central to what happened, first-person is necessarily and legitimately used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral clarity / clear point of view when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: A story may present a clear moral stance or point of view if that clarity strengthens the work's purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elizabeth Bruenig's work is cited for moral clarity; judges value when point of view is integral and clearly argued, provided reporting supports it rather than substituting for evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact and public consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Features that produce tangible impact (policy change, public attention, institutional responses) are especially notable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a series that led to a temporary moratorium on the death penalty. Impact is not required but strengthens a story's significance for awards and recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic production expectations given resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize differences in time and resources between newsroom types (newspapers vs. magazines) when judging ambition and execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DeGregory observes that magazine writers often have more time/resources; newspaper writers compete against outlets like The Atlantic or The New Yorker but may have constraints. Judges may consider context and resource limits when evaluating work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building trust with sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing and maintaining source trust is a core part of producing quality feature journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presentation includes 'tricks and tips for building trust with sources' (details in linked webinar). Implicit guidance: deep sourcing and relationships enable the immersive scenes and reporting that features require.
